## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/03.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Academic Recovery in 2023
• The availability of 2023 RISE/UA+ data allows Utah to update
 COVID-19 recovery analyses.
• Spring 2023 marks the third year since the pandemic began
 and this allows for the third set of analyses to be presented:
 • Summer 2021: Academic Impact
 • Summer 2022: Academic Recovery Year 1
 • Summer 2023: Academic Recovery Year 2

 3</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/04.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Two Types of Recovery in 2023: System &amp; Student
• We elaborate on the results from the previous recovery analyses in two ways:
 • System level recovery: Is the education system supporting rates of
 learning that are comparable to what it was prior to the pandemic?
 • Student level recovery: Are students achieving at levels that are
 comparable to what they were prior to the pandemic?
• Originally, we focused mostly on system-level recovery: examining rates of
 learning in 2021 and 2022 compared to those prior to the pandemic.
• We continue examining system level analyses but also focus on student-level
 recovery.
 • The reason for providing both is to counter a prevailing narrative that the
 education system continues to suffer because students lag behind their
 pre-pandemic levels of attainment.
 4</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/05.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Two Types of Recovery: System &amp; Student
• System-level recovery
 • Comparison of 2019 and 2023 same-grade student growth: We
 examined the change in baseline student growth (SGPs) for 2019
 students and 2023 students utilizing coefficient matrices derived
 from pre-pandemic cohorts of students.
• Student-level recovery
 • Comparison of 2019 to 2023 same-grade achievement: We
 examine the equi-percentile change in achievement for 2019
 students and 2023 students at same-grade

 5</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/06.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">System-level recovery
• It is better to understand the health of the education system via the
 rates of student learning that it supports rather than the level of
 student attainment that are evident.
• Because students’ rates of learning slowed so dramatically during the
 pandemic, rates of learning necessary to catch students up to where
 they would have been would have to be equally dramatic (in the
 opposite direction)
 • That is, the system could return to producing normal rates of
 learning without students recovering.

 6</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/07.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Student-level recovery
• Student level recovery is the most common representation of recovery
 presented in the media: Where are students now compared to where
 they were in 2019.
• Comparison to 2019 attainment levels is a “low bar” for comparison:
 • Attainment levels in 2023, had the pandemic not occurred, would
 almost certainly have been higher than 2019 levels (based on
 “typical” rates of yearly improvement)
• In the following we provide data indicating the extent to which student
 attainment is behind 2019 attainment levels.

 7</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/10.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Why Baseline SGPs?
• Why does one need to look at baseline referenced SGPs instead of, for example,
 scale score gains. There are several reasons.
 • SGPs are the growth metric that the state of Utah has been using for more
 than a decade.
 • SGPs are readily interpretable probabilistically whereas gain scores are not.
 • Quantile regression (on which SGPs are based) is invariant to mono-tone
 transformations of scale (equi-variant to mono-tone transformations of
 scale). OLS regression, for example, is not. See Koenker (2005, p. 38)
 • Gain scores (which can be calculated since RISE is vertically scaled) are
 dependent upon: Content area, grade, prior level of achievement.
 • Gain scores were largely discredited as an effective means of communicating
 change. For example, no state uses them as a growth model.

 10</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/12.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Impact Phase
• Student growth (baseline referenced to pre-pandemic rates of
 learning) was examined by content area and grade as well as for the
 major student demographic subgroups.
• Impact was categorized as ranging from Severe to Modest to None.
• For almost all content areas and grades, impact was categorized as
 moderate (-0.25 &lt;= effect size &lt;= -0.1/ -15 &lt;= median SGP decrease &lt;=
 -5.

 12</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/16.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Recovery Phase Year 1
• Student growth (baseline referenced to pre-pandemic rates of learning)
 was examined by content area and grade as well as for the major student
 demographic subgroups.
• Achievement (Student Recovery) and Growth (System Recovery) were
 characterized in three ways:
 • Lagging: Behind pre-pandemic levels (attainment or growth)
 • On Par: About the same as pre-pandemic levels (attainment or growth)
 • Leading: Ahead of pre-pandemic levels (attainment or growth)
• Because learning slowed during the initial phase of the pandemic (2020 to
 2021), to make up for those losses, learning must accelerate to rates
 above normal (i.e., leading)
 16</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/21.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Recovery Year 1
• Analysis of 2022 RISE data indicated several positive trends in Utah to be happy
 about.
• In both ELA and mathematics, learning acceleration was at least as much to be
 considered stabilization and in many cases could be considered as genuine
 recovery.
• Compared to a dozen other states that the Center conducts these analyses, Utah
 comes out as the best in terms of pandemic recovery.
• Despite a robust recovery, students remain slightly behind 2019 levels in ELA and
 more in mathematics.</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/39.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Recovery Year 2
• Analysis of 2023 RISE data indicates two things:
 • Rates of learning, on average, are slightly exceeding or at pre-pandemic rates of
 growth. That is, the system has recovered, and then some.
 • Student attainment, on average, is still lagging behind because rates of learning have
 not accelerated enough to catch students up. That is, students have not fully
 “recovered” but levels are, in most grades, close to pre-pandemic levels.
• In both ELA and mathematics, learning acceleration from the lows of the pandemic would
 be considered, on average. That is, the system has stabilized.

 39</div>
```
